title: Postpone your rumination window
summary: Park repetitive thoughts in one fixed daily window so they stop running the rest of your day.
steps: Notice when the same thought keeps coming back.
Write that thought down in one short sentence.
Tell yourself you will think about it later, at a time you choose.
Pick a fixed 15-minute window today as your thinking time.
When the thought returns before then, say 'later' and go back to what you were doing.
sources: Stenzel et al. 2025, Psychological Medicine (meta-analysis: rumination-focused interventions)

title: Move from 'why' to 'what' and 'how'
summary: Shift abstract 'why' questions into concrete facts and next steps you can actually act on.
steps: Write down the 'why' question your mind keeps asking.
Rewrite it as a 'what happened' question with specific facts.
List two concrete details you can point to, not interpretations.
Ask 'what is one small next step' instead of 'why does this keep happening'.
Read your concrete version aloud once.
sources: Stenzel et al. 2025, Psychological Medicine (meta-analysis: rumination-focused interventions)

title: Notice the loop, then refocus
summary: Catch rumination in the act and deliberately point your attention at something engaging.
steps: Name it when you notice it: 'I am ruminating again'.
Stop and take one slow breath.
Choose an activity that holds your attention for a few minutes.
Give that activity your full focus, minute by minute.
If the loop returns, notice it again and redirect once more.
sources: Stenzel et al. 2025, Psychological Medicine (meta-analysis: rumination-focused interventions)

title: Schedule small activities
summary: Plan small, concrete activities for the coming days — one for mastery, one for pleasure — and do them.
steps: Open your calendar for the next three days.
Choose one small task that gives a sense of accomplishment.
Choose one small activity you usually enjoy.
Write both into specific time slots.
After each one, mark whether you did it and how it felt.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Take one values-direction step
summary: Pick one direction that matters to you and take one small step toward it today.
steps: Name one area of life that matters to you: relationships, work, health, or play.
Picture what acting on that value would look like this week.
Shrink it to a step you can finish in ten minutes.
Do the step now, or put it in your calendar.
Write one sentence about what it was like.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Map mood to activity
summary: Track the link between what you do and how you feel, then repeat the activities that help.
steps: Three times today, note what you are doing and rate your mood from 0 to 10.
Keep each entry short and specific.
At day's end, circle the activities that came with a higher mood.
Underline the activities that came with a lower mood.
Plan to repeat one helpful activity tomorrow.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Take a self-compassion break
summary: Meet a hard moment with three simple lines: acknowledge it, remember you are not alone, offer yourself kindness.
contraindications: This exercise is not for processing traumatic memories; if trauma memories surface, pause and seek support from a professional.
steps: Stop and say to yourself: 'this is a hard moment'.
Say: 'hard moments happen to everyone'.
Say: 'may I be kind to myself right now'.
Rest a hand on your chest if it helps the words feel real.
Repeat once whenever the harshness returns.
sources: Krieger et al. 2019 (online compassion training for self-criticism)
Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Notice the harsh inner voice
summary: Catch and name the harsh inner voice so it has less say over your next action.
contraindications: This exercise can surface painful self-judgements; if distress rises, pause and seek support from a professional.
steps: Catch the moment your inner voice turns harsh.
Write down the exact sentence it said.
Label it: 'that is self-criticism'.
Ask what you would say to a friend in the same spot.
Say that sentence to yourself once, out loud.
sources: Krieger et al. 2019 (online compassion training for self-criticism)

title: Remember common humanity
summary: Remind yourself that struggle is part of being human, not evidence of personal failure.
contraindications: This exercise is not for processing traumatic memories; if trauma memories surface, pause and seek support from a professional.
steps: Notice the thought that you are the only one struggling.
Say: 'many people feel this way today'.
Say: 'this does not mean I am broken or failing'.
Name one person you care about who has had a hard week.
Let yourself off the hook for one small thing.
sources: Krieger et al. 2019 (online compassion training for self-criticism)
Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Savor one moment
summary: Slow down one pleasant moment on purpose so it actually lands in your day.
steps: Pick one pleasant moment you are having right now.
Slow it down: look, listen, and feel it for a full minute.
Say one sentence about why you like it.
Let the moment be good without hunting for the catch.
Write one line about it tonight.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Try another reading
summary: Revisit a straining situation and look for one other reading of it that also fits the facts.
steps: Write the situation in one plain sentence.
Write the harshest interpretation you are holding about it.
Write a second interpretation that also fits the facts.
Write a third if you can, and keep only what matches the facts.
Notice which reading leaves you steadier, and choose it.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)

title: Break one problem into steps
summary: Turn one nagging problem into a short list of doable steps instead of circling it in your head.
steps: Write the problem as one plain sentence.
List every possible action, however small.
Cross out the actions you cannot do right now.
Pick the first doable action and give it a time today.
Do it, then decide the next step.
sources: Tong et al. 2024, EBioMedicine (meta-analysis: self-guided digital interventions)
